query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (approximately 1–2 atomic percent) of tungsten to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance its resistance to room-temperature creep and improve its overall performance under extreme temperature fluctuations and long-term mechanical loading compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure produced by conventional casting and processing routes.
generation.intervention: Alloying modification by incorporating ~1–2 at.% tungsten into the base alloy during melting and homogenization, while maintaining the same processing route to retain the lamellar microstructure.
generation.conditions: Both the tungsten-modified and baseline alloys are processed identically (melt, cast, homogenize, and controlled cooling to preserve the fine lamellar structure) and then tested under service conditions that simulate extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion environments.
generation.structural_mediator: W segregation at the lamellar interfaces is expected to stabilize these boundaries and inhibit mechanisms such as grain-boundary sliding and diffusion-controlled creep.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition is hypothesized to strengthen the lamellar interfaces by segregating to these regions, thereby impeding dislocation motion and reducing diffusional creep processes. This stabilization may also improve the corrosion resistance by helping to preserve a more uniform and chemically stable interphase, contributing to the overall improved practical performance of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The primary measured property is the room-temperature creep rate, which is predicted to decrease relative to the baseline alloy. Improvements in high-temperature strength and maintenance (or slight enhancement) of ductility are also expected, though the precise magnitude of these improvements is uncertain.
generation.baseline: The standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy without tungsten addition, processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected only when the lamellar structure is preserved through controlled processing, and under the specified testing conditions simulating extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion. Outside these prescribed conditions, the effects are uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in creep resistance and strength is uncertain due to potential complex interactions within the alloy matrix. Additionally, while the hypothesis targets enhanced performance, there is some uncertainty regarding the precise impact on ductility, which requires empirical validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and one set with ~1–2 at.% tungsten added. Ensure both sets follow the same melting, homogenization, and controlled cooling processes to maintain the fine lamellar structure. Subject samples to standardized room-temperature creep tests under a constant load (and appropriate duration) and corrosion tests (e.g., using a salt spray or equivalent environment).
measurements: Yield strength at room and elevated temperatures
Corrosion rate in the designated testing environment
Microstructural analysis to verify tungsten segregation at lamellar interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the creep rate (or an improvement in key performance metrics such as yield strength and corrosion resistance) compared to the baseline, or if the modification results in an unacceptable reduction in ductility, then the hypothesis is falsified.
